clue.text: Father has engagement in possibly vulgar part

parts.note: FR is the standard abbreviation for Father, as a priest's title
an engagement is a battle, which is military action

explanation.surface: A priest gets drawn into some crude business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vulgar' points at bad taste, but a vulgar fraction is the schoolroom name for one written as numerator over denominator; 'possibly' marks it as one kind among several.
explanation.definitionFit: A vulgar fraction is a part of a whole written as one number over another, so the definition gives an example of the type.

clue.text: Sweet-talk for even a heartless man

parts.note: even means level or flat

indicators.note: heartless says the middle of the man's name is cut out

parts.note: Terry is a man's name

explanation.surface: Charming words for a cold-hearted fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' drops the central R of TERRY to give TERY; 'for' and 'a' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet-talk is insincere praise used to win someone over, which is what blandishment amounts to.

clue.text: Handy girl has power to accept one pound

indicators.note: to accept means the girl and the powerful word take in another piece between them

parts.note: Ava is a girl's name
someone able has the power or capacity to do something
I is the Roman numeral one
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A capable young woman is strong enough to take a single quid.
explanation.walkthrough: IL slots in where AVA meets ABLE. L for pound comes from the Latin libra, as in the £ sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handy is close at hand and ready for use, which means it can be had.

clue.text: Some of the Irish are possessive!

indicators.note: Some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of the population of Ireland are said to be jealous types.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possessive' is the grammar sense: a possessive pronoun or adjective, not a jealous person.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatically a possessive word shows ownership, and this one is the plural third-person form used before a noun.

clue.text: Displeases, having bad intentions

parts.note: food that is off has gone bad
ends are aims or intentions, as in the ends justify the means

explanation.surface: Someone annoys people by acting with malicious motives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having bad intentions' looks like a description of a villain, but splits into two synonyms; 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To give offence is to upset or annoy someone, so the verb matches displeases.

clue.text: Poet's girl taking a break after six

indicators.note: after says the reworked girl follows the six

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: breaking the word girl apart lets its letters be put back in a new order

explanation.surface: A young woman takes time off once six o'clock comes round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking a break' sounds like a rest from work, but it signals the anagram: GIRL becomes RGIL, placed after VI. The 's of 'Poet's' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of the Aeneid is among the most celebrated poets of antiquity.

clue.text: Animal alleged to cause crocodile tears?

definitions.text: Animal alleged to cause crocodile tears?

parts.words: Animal alleged to cause crocodile tears?
parts.note: ancient legend held that a mongoose-like creature of Egypt crept into a sleeping crocodile's mouth and ate its way out, which would surely make the reptile weep

explanation.surface: Which beast is supposed to make crocodiles cry?
explanation.walkthrough: Crocodile tears normally means fake sorrow; here a crocodile has real cause to cry, from the old fable of the Egyptian mongoose.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian mongoose, an animal of fable said to attack crocodiles from inside, is what the clue describes.

clue.text: Head of the groundsmen left the county

indicators.note: Head of picks out the first letter of the groundsmen

parts.note: left in the sense departed means went

explanation.surface: The chief groundsman has walked out of the county ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' is the past of leave, WENT, not the opposite of right. GWENT is a former county in south-east Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A former county in south-east Wales bears this name, so the definition names its category.

clue.text: Not quite the ultimate vehicle for a sailor

indicators.note: not quite means the word for the ultimate stops one letter short

parts.note: the ultimate thing is the last one
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Something falls just short of being the best car for a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' trims LAST to LAS. A lascar is a sailor from India or South-East Asia, a word from British imperial shipping.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar was an East Indian seaman serving on European ships, so the definition names his trade.

clue.text: "Nile spills his overflow Beside the — 's dead" (Housman)

definitions.text: "Nile spills his overflow Beside the — 's dead" (Housman)

parts.words: "Nile spills his overflow Beside the — 's dead" (Housman)
parts.note: a line from A Shropshire Lad where the poet sets the Egyptian river beside a river of his own Shropshire landscape

explanation.surface: A gap-fill quotation from A. E. Housman's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank wants a river: Housman's A Shropshire Lad contrasts the Nile with Britain's longest river, which flows through Shropshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Housman's line names Britain's longest river, which flows past Shrewsbury in Shropshire, the county of his famous poems.

clue.text: Conscious of article by the path

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
a wake is the track or path a ship leaves on the water

explanation.surface: Someone is aware of a definite article standing by a footpath.
explanation.walkthrough: WAKE is the path a vessel cuts through water; 'of' and 'by' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone conscious is not asleep, which is the plain sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Originality of new head

parts.note: something new is fresh
a ness is a headland, a head of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Innovation comes from a newly appointed boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' reads as a leader, but NESS is a geographical head, a promontory, as in Loch Ness's neighbouring place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Originality and novelty go together: work that is original has a newness about it.

clue.text: Permitted variation of an uncommonly clear note

indicators.note: uncommonly says the letters of clear note come in an unusual order

explanation.surface: An engineer allows some leeway for a strangely clear musical note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' turns CLEAR NOTE into the answer; 'of an' is link material.
explanation.definitionFit: In engineering, the allowed margin by which a measurement may differ from its nominal value is called its tolerance range.

clue.text: Run to get more

explanation.surface: Sprint to earn a bit more.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a run scored without the bat touching the ball, such as a wide or a bye, is counted separately as an extra.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket run off byes or wides is scored separately from the batter's tally; and something additional is more than the usual amount.

clue.text: Burglars insert key in dressers

indicators.note: insert ... in tells us to put one piece inside the people who dress others

parts.note: a rober is one who robes, or dresses, someone
B is a musical key

explanation.surface: Housebreakers slip a key into chests of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressers' looks like furniture, but here it means people who robe others, ROBERS; the musical key B goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Burglars and robbers are both thieves who take other people's property.

clue.text: Anne cured disorder in 12

indicators.note: disorder says the letters of Anne cured are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: A woman named Anne got over her illness through sheer patience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorder' looks like an illness Anne was cured of, but it signals the anagram; '12' refers to 12 across, TOLERANCE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance in its sense of putting up with hardship is close to stamina and the capacity to bear things.

clue.text: Count of ten, perhaps, for this knock-out

explanation.surface: A referee counts to ten over a boxer flattened by a knockout punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the answer as 'more numb', the state a knock-out blow leaves a boxer in; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten is a figure, an example of a counting value; and a knock-out blow leaves a boxer feeling deader and less sensitive than before.

clue.text: Knowledge gained from issue about: football

indicators.note: about says the word for an issue goes round another piece

parts.note: an edition is an issue of a newspaper or book
RU stands for Rugby Union, a code of football

explanation.surface: An expert's learning comes from an edition about soccer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'football' suggests soccer, but RU is Rugby Union, a form of football; 'gained from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudition is deep learning, scholarship acquired by study, so it is a form of knowledge.

clue.text: Lively lady got married, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: Anna is a woman's name; mated means paired off, coupled

explanation.surface: A cheerful woman got wed, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'Anna mated' quickly and it sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively and animated both describe someone full of energy and spirit.

clue.text: Information given to communist in return for sex

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: in return says the word for a communist is turned backwards

parts.note: a red is a communist

explanation.surface: A spy hands secrets to a Marxist in exchange for sexual favours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' sounds like an exchange, but it turns the communist backwards; 'given to' is a link, and the Marxist's colour comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar and biology both classify by sex, as male or female, and that classification is also called gender.

clue.text: Novelist is right to become senior lecturer

parts.note: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth

explanation.surface: A writer of fiction is entitled to be promoted at the university.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade wrote Victorian novels. In British universities a reader ranks just below professor.
explanation.definitionFit: At a British university, the post above senior lecturer and below professor carries this title.

clue.text: King maybe who doesn't fly

explanation.surface: A monarch who will not travel by air.
explanation.walkthrough: The king is a species of seabird from the Antarctic, not a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The king is one species of flightless Antarctic seabird; and all of that bird family are unable to fly.

clue.text: Being no end blue in this country

indicators.note: no end means the last letter of the shade of blue is dropped

parts.note: Prussian blue is a deep blue pigment

explanation.surface: Someone is endlessly sad in their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end blue' looks like 'extremely sad', but means PRUSSIAN (as in Prussian blue) losing its final N. 'Being' and 'in this' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Prussia was a former German kingdom and state, so the definition names its category.

clue.text: Assume to be iron? In fact, wrong

indicators.note: wrong says the letters are put together incorrectly, in a jumbled order

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: Someone presumes something to be iron, but is in fact mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' shuffles FE with FACT. 'Assume' here is to put on a manner, as in assuming an air; 'to be' and 'In' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To affect an accent is to put it on or pretend to it, which is to assume it.

clue.text: Part of Lourdes meal

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters inside the words of Lourdes

explanation.surface: Some food served in the French pilgrimage town of Lourdes.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in 'of', taking its last letter, and continues into 'Lourdes'. 'meal' here is ground grain, not a dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Meal is coarsely ground grain, and the finely ground form used for baking is its close relative.

clue.text: Neat word, almost, for the armpit

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, and an ox is one

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word for a word is left off

parts.note: a term is a word or expression

explanation.surface: A tidy word for the underarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' is an archaic word for cattle, hence OX; 'almost' trims TERM. OXTER is a Scots and northern English word for armpit.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland and northern England the hollow under the arm goes by this dialect name.

clue.text: Graduates, including one retired classical character, discover element

indicators.note: including says the word for graduates holds another piece within it

parts.note: alumni are former students, graduates of a school or university
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: retired means the Greek letter goes back, so it is read in reverse

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: Former students, with a retired lecturer in Classics, make a scientific discovery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' reads as a pensioned scholar, but it means the Greek letter goes backwards to finish the word; 'discover' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A light silvery metal, number 13 in the periodic table, is a chemical element.

clue.text: It's not fitting to sleep in the thing

indicators.note: in says the short sleep goes inside the word for the thing

parts.note: it is a word for the thing being spoken of
a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: Dozing off in the middle of something is inappropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is a link meaning 'it is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsuitable or out of place for the occasion is said to be inapt.

clue.text: Late offers for paint additives

parts.note: late in the sense former is ex, as in an ex-husband
tenders are formal offers or bids

explanation.surface: Some last-minute bids for supplies used in decorating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' means former here, EX, not tardy.
explanation.definitionFit: Additives used to bulk out paint cheaply stretch it further, which is what extending agents do.

clue.text: Take in livestock to make a point

parts.note: the gist is the main point of something

explanation.surface: A farmer puts animals out to graze to prove an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: To agist is a farming term for taking in other people's livestock to graze for a fee; 'to make' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmer who grazes others' animals on his land for payment is said to agist them, an old legal and agricultural term.

clue.text: Goal for a sailor to achieve

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
to get something is to achieve or obtain it

explanation.surface: A seaman sets out the aim he hopes to reach.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR, short for tarpaulin, is the crossword's favourite sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A goal is an aim or objective, something you set out to hit.

clue.text: Soccer authority's one short of a team — Edward's tied up

parts.note: the FA is the Football Association, English soccer's governing body, with its possessive S
a football team has eleven players, and one fewer is ten
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: The Football Association, a player short, has bound Edward hand and foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The FA is England's Football Association; its 's supplies an S. A soccer side is eleven, so one short is TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tied up has been secured or fixed in place with a knot or fastening.
